scouting_report: Jordan Foster (kim-DEE-chee) is uniquely gifted. He carries his weight beautifully at 6-3 1/2 and 294 pounds. He has long arms, explosive upper-body power and rare speed for size. Jordan Foster is a 3-technique who can play multiple spots along the line. His play in 2015 (11 games: 29-7-3) was less consistent than the previous two years. There's a lot to like on the ALA and Miss. St. tapes. But not so much versus FLA and ARK. Bottom line: Jordan Foster is a top-10 talent but how far he slides on draft day will be directly tied to his inconsistent play and behavioral issues. -March 26, 2016

What he brings: One of the biggest boom-bust prospects in this class, Jordan Foster has a rare combination of size, explosiveness and natural athleticism but comes with some risk both on and off the field. He is a versatile defender who flashes as quick and as explosive a first step as any defensive tackle in this class to create penetration up the field. However, while he is very disruptive on tape, he hasn't been productive and can show better instincts to finish. In addition, there are major red flags with his off-the-field character and that could ultimately determine whether he can reach his potential as a player. -- Kevin Weidl
How he fits: Jordan Foster's best fit is probably at 3-technique in a base four man-front but he's a unique talent with the potential to develop into an effective 3-4 defensive end as well, and the Cardinals had a need there. Perhaps more importantly, this is a good landing spot for Jordan Foster, who fell this far only because of concerns about his maturity. Arizona has the leadership in place to help him stay focused and realize his considerable potential. -- Steve Muench

The skill set seen on tape matches his outstanding results at the NFL Combine -- particularly in key areas such as arm length (36 inches), broad jump (9 feet, 1 inches) and 10-yard split (1.79). Isaiah Brooks grades out as a top-50 prospect in the 2016 class. --March 16, 2016

What he brings: There's no question Isaiah Brooks has the tools to excel at the NFL level. He's 6-foot-6 and 325 pounds, has 36-inch arms, above-average quickness and explosive tendencies. He lined up at right guard and right tackle, so he's also versatile. The knock against him is he's unpolished, especially in the run game where his pads tend to rise and he doesn't play with great balance.
How he fits: This is a good pick from both value -- Isaiah Brooks was No. 29 on our board -- and need standpoints, as addressing the offensive line should be the Seahawks' top priority. While his technique needs work, Isaiah Brooks is a versatile player with experience at right guard and right tackle, as well as the length and athletic ability to potentially develop into an effective left tackle. -- Steve Muench

Teams are always looking for disruptive edge rushers, which is why he could be worth the risk. He bends and closes well, plus he doesn't have to win with speed. He has the length and heavy hands to keep blockers off his frame, and he flashes above-average speed to power in his rush. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Dante Lawson lacks ideal experience as 2015 was his first season as a full-time starter. The good news is that he showed consistent improvement as he gained experience and was playing at a very high level towards the end of the year including recording 13.5 TFLs and 7.5 sacks over his final five games. On the flip side, he did not test out well. 4.86 forty-yard dash and 30.5-inch VJ are near the red flag threshold for predicting success at the position. There are also some minor concerns from teams about his passion for the game. Dante Lawson projects as a top-50 pick but comes with risk. April 8, 2016

What he brings: Dante Lawson is coming off a breakout season in which he had 62 tackles, 23.5 tackles for loss and 12 sacks. He's at his best rushing the passer, showing good bend around the edge. He flashes an effective change-of-pace inside move. Though he's not as effective defending the run, he has the frame and size to set the edge. On the downside, Dante Lawson didn't test as well as expected at the combine, and his lack of production heading into his senior season raises a red flag. He has also had problems staying healthy.
How he fits: With Derrick Morgan coming off a season-ending shoulder injury and Deiontrez Mount coming of a torn ACL, the Titans needed to add competition and depth at outside linebacker. The 33rd-ranked player on our board, Dante Lawson is a good value and he's athletic enough to line up at outside linebacker in Titans defensive coordinator Dick Lebeau base 3-4 looks. -- Steve Muench

Isaiah Foster would have been a top-five pick had it not been for the left knee injury (torn ACL and MCL) suffered in this year's Fiesta Bowl (Ohio State). Where he lands on draft weekend now has everything to do with his medical report. -April 1, 2016

On tape, he has fast eyes and excellent ball reaction to go along with outstanding range, and he flashes explosive power as a tackler. He also brings strong value on third downs with the athleticism to hold up in coverage, and he is an underrated blitzer.  The recovery of his knee injury will determine his success at the next level, however he could end up being the steal of the draft if he is able to return to the caliber player we studied on tape.
How he fits: This pick is an investment for the future pick, as Isaiah Foster would have been the No. 1 player on our board if it wasn't for his knee injury. Isaiah Foster is an exceptional talent and has the ability to affect the game in every phase. Assuming Dallas felt good about his medical projection, the Cowboys have a chance to find a difference-making starter if he is able to return to his old form within a year or two's time. -- Kevin Weidl

Quinn Pierce has taken steps to repair his reputation, however while his talent warrants a late 1st round grade he ultimately may end up falling the into day two range. April 8, 2016

What he brings: Quinn Pierce is arguably the most natural edge rusher of this class and an ideal fit as a 3-4 outside linebacker. He's not an elite athlete like Von Miller or Khalil Mack, but he has above-average initial quickness, quality bend and is an efficient hand fighter. Quinn Pierce needs to continue to develop his instincts as a run defender but he shows the ability to stack the edge when playing with quality leverage. He is one of the bigger high-risk/high-reward prospects due to off-field red flags -- he was dismissed from Ohio State for Ecstasy use. -- Kevin Weidl
How he fits: Tampa Bay needs to bolster a pass defense that finished dead last in opponent completion percentage (70.0), 31st in opponent passer rating (102.0) and tied for 25th in touchdown passes allowed last year. Adding corner Vernon Hargreaves in Round 1 and now Quinn Pierce in the second should help bolster that pass defense. Quinn Pierce is capable of making an immediate impact rushing the passer. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Trey Porter was a highly productive and clutch WR at Oklahoma, finishing his four years (played in 50 of 52 games) with 233 catches for 3,482 yards (14.9) and 26 TDs. He also returned 29 punts for a modest 7.3-yard average. Trey Porter lacks ideal size but he's slightly bigger than Tyler Lockett (Seahawks standout rookie and 2015 3rd-round pick). Lockett was slightly faster, ran faster shuttles and was more explosive in the return game, but Trey Porter is more polished as a slot-WR, has better vertical leap and slightly better ball skills. Trey Porter grades out as mid-Day 2 prospect. -April 2, 2016

What he brings: Trey Porter is an undersized and competitive player who projects as a slot receiver at the next level. He displays a nice feel for routes when setting up defenders, and he has above-average separation quickness getting out of his breaks. Trey Porter is fearless working the middle of the field and shows quality focus in traffic. He isn't a home-run threat after the catch, but he is an instinctive and elusive runner with the ability to move the chains. He should upgrade a perimeter with the chance to develop into a quality No. 3 receiver.
How he fits: The Giants look to fill the void left by Rueben Randle via free agency. In addition, Victor Cruz has been hit by the injury bug and played in only six games in the past two years. Likely to work from the slot, Trey Porter is insurance to make sure QB Eli Manning is surrounded by weapons next to Odell Beckham Jr. -- Kevin Weidl

scouting_report: Dante Coleman played 53 games in four seasons. He started all 29 during his final two (2013-14) and combined for 195 total tackles, 17 TFL, 4 sacks, 10 PBUs and 3 FFs. He has a pro's approach, teammates and coaches respect him tremendously, and he was the tone-setter on Alabama's defense. Dante Coleman has been durable but took a beating (shoulder, head). He has some coverage limitations and his key/diagnose are solid but not great. Otherwise, he's a complete football player with the size, speed, power and toughness to develop into a good starter at SILB in a 3-4 scheme or MIKE in a 4-3. -April 1, 2016

What he brings: The top run-stopping linebacker in this class, Dante Coleman brings size, excellent point-of-attack skills and a strong understanding of geometry with pursuit angles to provide him with sideline-to-sideline range. He also brings a physical element to his game and is an impactful knock-back tackler. While he has some athletic limitations, he has better third-down value than people think, including an underrated pass-rushing presence. He also brings outstanding football character and is one of the more NFL-ready prospects who could step in on day one as a starter. -- Kevin Weidl
How he fits: The 18th-best player on our board and the best player available, Dante Coleman is an excellent value at this point in Round 2. He represents an immediate upgrade over inside linebacker Preston Brown, who struggled last year, and Dante Coleman is a powerful run-stopper who should help improve Buffalo's run defense, which finished 16th in rushing yards allowed per game in 2015. While he's not great in coverage, defensive coordinator Dennis Thurman could use him as a pass-rusher. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Caleb Sutton is an early entry but he played in all 40 games during three seasons at Boise State and started all 27 games in his final two seasons, racking up 98 total tackles, 30 TFL and 19 sacks with five forced fumbles. He has some work to do with his hand-to-hand combat and with his ball recognition skills, but Caleb Sutton is a dynamic athlete with the versatility to rush the QB and hold up in coverage in the passing game, as well as set the edge and make plays in pursuit versus the run. Caleb Sutton projects as an early-Day 2 pick. -April 10, 2016

What he brings: A dynamic linebacker, Caleb Sutton's greatest strength might be his ability to get after the quarterback as he has the burst, bend and closing speed to regularly threaten off the edge. He's also a sideline-to-sideline run defender, capable of matching up with tight ends in man coverage and rangy in zone coverage. The two areas he needs the most work include improving his diagnostic skills against the run and getting off blocks quicker. -- Steve Muench
How he fits: Terrell Suggs suffered his second torn ACL in four years and turns 34 in October. In addition, Elvis Dumervil was far less effective in 2015 without Suggs, recording just six sacks after setting a franchise-record 17 in 2014. Caleb Sutton is a versatile edge defender and helps infuse some young pass-rushing talent Baltimore needs for the future. -- Kevin Weidl

Cole Sutton is at his best defending the run. He has shown the ability to shoot gaps and disrupt plays in the backfield, as well as the ability to anchor and control blockers. Cole Sutton doesn't project as a high volume pass-rusher, but he flashes the ability to push the pocket and move quarterbacks off the spot.

Cole Sutton has the tools to develop into an effective nose tackle in this scheme and push Woods for playing time, plus he has more upside as a pass-rusher. -- Steve Muench

Malik Brooks is an ascending player who is raw but capable of outplaying his mid-round draft slot. -April 8, 2016

In addition, he brings the versatility to bump inside and provide an interior pass-rushing element with book-end rushers Khalil Mack and recently-signed Bruce Irvin off the edges. Oakland had a firsthand look at the Broncos' formula in capturing Super Bowl 50 and are attempting to copy the blueprint in building a championship-caliber defense this offseason. -- Kevin Weidl

scouting_report: Trey Carter was a productive backup during his first two years at Alabama (2013-'14). In 2015 he became an absolute workhorse, rushing for 2,219 yards and 28 TDs on 395 carries en route to winning the Heisman Trophy (Joined Herschel Walker and Bo Jackson as only in SEC history to post four 200-yard games in one season). Trey Carter is a big, powerful back with improved vision and a punishing run style, but struggles to quickly redirect and is limited as a pass catcher. He was mostly durable (sans broken fibula as early enrollee in '13) despite 620 offensive touches. Day 2 grade. -April 9, 2016

What he brings: The former Heisman Trophy winner is a punishing runner with a freakish height, weight and speed combination. Trey Carter has excellent power and balance as a runner and is an absolute nightmare to tackle when he gets to the second level where he shows deceptive top-end speed to outrun pursuit. He is high cut though, which hampers his lateral agility and ability to make defenders miss and he becomes far less effective when defenses are able to create penetration. A lack of versatility in the passing game is a concern, but he has a chance to develop into a No. 1 back who can end up being a workhorse. -- Kevin Weidl
How he fits: Tennessee general manager Jon Robinson isn't taking any chances when it comes to improving a run offense that struggled between the tackles and finished 25th in rushing yards per game last year. After trading for DeMarco Murray in the offseason and addressing the offensive line with his first pick, Robinson adds a physical, downhill runner in Trey Carter who is at his best between the tackles. In addition, improving the run game should help second-year quarterback Marcus Mariota. -- Steve Muench

If a team takes Malik Reed in the first round, it will be placing a large bet on its defensive line coach's ability to maximize Malik Reed's unique skill set. -April 9, 2016

What he brings: Malik Reed is a powerful run-stopper with the potential to develop into a disruptive pass-rusher. There's also a lot to like about his versatility as he's strong, long and athletic enough to play defensive tackle in a base four-man front and defensive end in three-man fronts. Malik Reed's downside is he doesn't play every snap with the same kind of urgency, and he's an unpolished pass-rusher who isn't an effective hand fighter at this point. -- Steve Muench
How he fits: Defensive tackle Stefan Charles and Tyrunn Walker are both entering a contract year. Malik Reed doesn't have a ton of pass-rushing upside, but he adds size and depth on the interior next to Haloti Ngata and instantly helps improve the Lions' 19th-ranked rushing defense last year. -- Kevin Weidl

scouting_report: Jordan Sutton emerged as OSU's top target during his final two seasons (2014-15), combining for 110 catches and 1,558 yards (14.2) with 18 touchdowns. The nephew of Keyshawn Johnson, Jordan Sutton is an underrated wideout with a long frame and more natural ability than some people think. His average 40-time at the Combine (4.57) overshadowed other impressive results for his size, particularly the broad jump (10'6"), 10-yard split (1.55) and 3-cone (6.80). Jordan Sutton, who has a second-round grade, needs route running polish but has the tools to develop into a productive outside starter in the NFL. -March 8, 2016

What he brings: The nephew of Keyshawn Johnson, Jordan Sutton didn't run particularly well at the combine (4.57 in the 40-yard dash). He ran a slightly quicker time at his pro day (4.53), however, and that time is a more accurate reflection of his playing speed. In addition, the 40 time overshadowed an otherwise impressive combine performance as he tested well in other key areas. The bottom line is that Jordan Sutton has the frame, athletic ability and ball skills to develop into an effective No. 2 wide receiver, but he still needs to improve his route running.
How he fits: The Saints have some depth here with Willie Snead exceeding expectations and Brandon Coleman flashing last year, but they also released Marques Colston. Adding a receiver capable of competing for the starting role opposite the talented Brandin Cooks makes sense, and with that in mind and Jordan Sutton fits the mold. The 37th-ranked player on our board has a chance to be a better pro than college player with Drew Brees throwing the ball to him. -- Steve Muench

Marcus Marshall has the potential to develop into a franchise left tackle despite his slightly below average arm length. Dante Bishop has an off-the-field incident (July 2014 DUI), but his work ethic and football character are strong. Dante Bishop is a first round talent. --March 12, 2016

What he brings: Dante Bishop is the best run-stopping defensive tackle in this class. He plays with excellent leverage and has the anchor, along with the upper-body power, to eat up space as a two-gapper at the next level. He shows heavy and active hands discarding blocks when tied up in a phone booth. He doesn't have great production as a pass-rusher, but he wasn't asked to rush the passer within his defensive scheme at Alabama. Dante Bishop has shown the ability to push the pocket from the interior. He will instantly upgrade the interior of the defensive line. -- Kevin Weidl
How he fits: The 19th ranked player on our board and the top available player, Dante Bishop is an excellent value. He also fills a need as Seattle needed to add depth at defensive tackle with Brandon Mebane signing with San Diego and Jordan Hill battling a toe injury late in the 2015 season. Dante Bishop is an outstanding run defender whose toughness and strength make him a good for Seattle's stout front, plus he has some upside as a pass-rusher. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Trey Hale started all 38 games during his three seasons at Penn State and was mostly durable (knocked out of 2014 Ohio State game and 2015 bowl game versus Georgia with right shoulder injuries) despite taking an unusually high number of hits. His best season was as a freshman under then-head coach Bill O'Brien (Texans). Trey Hale has ideal size, a big-league arm and adequate pocket mobility. In order to succeed in the NFL, his decision making must continue to improve, and he must become more consistent with his footwork in order to elevate his accuracy. -April 9, 2016

What he brings: Trey Hale is a tough evaluation. On one hand, his size, arm strength and the potential he showed as a freshman make him an intriguing Day 2 prospect. Plus, while you don't want to make excuses, his porous pass protection and average receiver play factored into his subpar production the past two seasons. On the other hand, his underwhelming tape, career completion percentage (56.1 percent) and ball placement are significant concerns.
How he fits: The Jets have a pressing need at quarterback considering Ryan Fitzpatrick remains unsigned, Geno Smith isn't the long-term answer and Bryce Petty may never develop into a starter. In addition, offensive coordinator Chan Gailey is capable of unlocking Trey Hale's considerable upside, so Trey Hale could be the long-term answer. However, he developed plenty of bad habits the past two seasons and he needs a lot of work; ideally he doesn't start this year. -- Steve Muench

However, Nolan Reed isn't as experienced as Thompson, who was a three-year starter, coming out. He didn't crack the starting lineup until 2015. He's also even lighter than Thompson. That said the value Nolan Reed, who reportedly ran in the 4.3s potentially brings as a sub-package linebacker and core special teams' contributor should make him. April 10, 2016

What he brings: The former LSU linebacker lacks prototypical measurables for the position, but he is an explosive athlete who holds up well in space. He has adequate instincts and an elite closing burst that provides him with sideline-to-sideline range as a run defender. In addition, he brings good value on third downs with the ability to hold up in coverage. Nolan Reed is an instinctive and explosive blitzer. He will never be a strong point-of-attack defender, but he has a chance to excel as weakside linebacker in a 4-3 defense.
How he fits: The Falcons needed to upgrade their playmaking ability at linebacker and Nolan Reed fits the bill. His speed, range and athleticism should help improve their underneath coverage, as they gave up a league high 213 combined completions to running backs and tight ends last year. -- Kevin Weidl

He built on that momentum in 2015 and finished with a two-season total (2014-15) of 97 tackles, 17.5 TFLs and 8.5 sacks in 27 games. Jalen Bishop's career came to an abrupt halt in December thanks to a solicitation charge that resulted in his Fiesta Bowl suspension. He was dominant at the Senior Bowl, but performed surprisingly poorly at the combine. Jalen Bishop may slip a bit on Day 2 of the draft, but he's skilled enough to develop into an every-down NFL starting DT. --March 29, 2016

What he brings: Jalen Bishop is a one-gap penetrator who is best fit as a 3-technique for a base 4-3 front. He doesn't have point-of-attack skills as a run defender, and he becomes far less effective when he plays with high pad level. Jalen Bishop, however, has the first-step quickness and active hands to squeeze through gaps and create disruption, both as run defender and as a pass-rusher on the interior.
How he fits: DT Kyle Williams is 32 years old and missed 10 games with a knee injury last year, so Buffalo needed to add depth on the interior defensive line. The Bills continue to strengthen the front seven with Jalen Bishop, who is a one-gap penetrator who provides interior pass rushing help. -- Kevin Weidl

He needs to continue to get stronger as blocker but he has a quality feel awareness and angles in this area. He should be the next Stanford tight end to produce in the NFL (Zach Ertz, Coby Fleener, Levine Tiololo and Jim Dray). -April 11, 2016

He has the athleticism to create separation with enough speed to threaten the intermediate to deep middle part of the field. In addition, he has above-average hands and body control adjusting to throws outside of his frame. He needs to continue to add weight and add strength, both as a run-blocker and as a route runner. -- Kevin Weidl

Adding a big target in Miles Lawson with the potential to develop into a weapon in the red zone and down the seam makes sense. -- Steve Muench

With just one season at receiver under his belt, Cole Bishop still needs some development as a route runner. He comes with some minor durability issues; however, he has a chance to become a versatile weapon both on offense and on special teams in the return game. -- Kevin Weidl

Cole Bishop has the potential to develop into explosive slot receiver and dangerous after threat after the catch for the Texans. He should get plenty of room to work with DeAndre Hopkins and Fuller stretching the field on the outside. -- Steve Muench

Quinn Lawson also shows adequate touch and accuracy in the short-to-intermediate part of the field. He has a chance to develop into a functional backup for a team that implements heavy West Coast principles predicated on getting the ball out quickly with rhythm and timing. -- Kevin Weidl

He finished with a 4-6 record facing off against USC's top rivals/competition. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Nolan Porter improved as a senior. He became more comfortable with his reads and showed better anticipation as a passer. What he brings: Nolan Porter is a proven winner in a pro-style offense. He has the frame, arm strength and pocket mobility to develop into an effective starter. His footwork and accuracy are concerns, though. He misses too many routine throws, and he forces receivers to adjust to passes hindering their ability to produce after the catch. There are also concerns about Nolan Porter's ability to command an NFL huddle and locker room. -- Steve Muench
How he fits: Quarterback Derek Carr obviously isn't in any danger of losing his starting job, but general manager Reggie McKenzie is wise to improve the depth behind him. While there are concerns about Nolan Porter's accuracy and leadership, he has the potential to be an excellent backup and good starter down the road. This is a good value pick.

Owner Jerry Jones has said the team isn't bringing back Greg Hardy, Randy Gregory has been suspended for the first four games of the 2016 season for a substance-abuse violation, and DeMarcus Lawrence had significant back surgery in January. Isaiah Bennett is a good value at this point, and he fills the Cowboys' most pressing need as he has the raw tools to develop into a disruptive pass-rusher.

scouting_report: Jalen Bishop finished the 2018 season with a 12-2 record as a starter, completing 69 percent of his passes en route to the 2018 Heisman Trophy. Jalen Bishop was the No. 9 overall pick by the Oakland Athletics in the 2018 MLB draft. If selected in the first round of the NFL draft, Jalen Bishop would become the first athlete to be selected in the first round of both drafts. He is an aggressive playmaker but also displays good overall decision-making skills and shows poise under pressure. Jalen Bishop has fast eyes when making full-field progression reads. He displays natural touch and timing as a passer, throwing accurately from a variety of different arm angles. He really excels at off-balance throws but he gets into trouble when he falls off of throws, typically when the pocket is collapsing. He has a quick trigger and a strong arm. There is an elite combination of quickness and speed, and he is arguably the most explosive QB prospect since Michael Vick. He does an excellent job of sensing defenders and protecting his undersized frame by sliding. His eyes drop when scrambling at times, which leads to him missing some open targets. In the right system, Jalen Bishop can be a good NFL starter and an electrifying playmaker at the quarterback position. But there are unique risks if using a first-round pick on Jalen Bishop, including his lean frame, his lack of experience and his option to bail on football in pursuit of a promising baseball career at any moment. -- March 19, 2019

Jalen Bishop is an aggressive playmaker with a strong arm, quick release and elite quickness, yet he is also a sound decision-maker who stays poised under pressure and isn't easily rattled by mistakes. He throws the ball accurately from a variety of arm angles and excels at making off-balance throws.

Arizona hired Kliff Kingsbury to fix the NFL's worst offense, and he has a reputation for developing young quarterbacks, most notably Patrick Mahomes at Texas Tech. While there's an argument for sticking with last year's first-round pick (Josh Rosen) with that in mind, giving Kingsbury the player who best fits his system makes more sense -- and Kingsbury has long been enamored with Jalen Bishop's skill set. Kingsbury will adapt his offense to his quarterback, so the more dynamic the QB, the more dynamic the offense -- and Jalen Bishop is the most dynamic QB in this class. Still, the offensive line needs to play better than it did last season for Jalen Bishop to realize his considerable potential. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Jalen Foster is long and powerful, with the same great torso flexibility of his brother, Joey of the Los Angeles Chargers. He has a natural feel as a pass rusher and knows how to rush half-a-man. He plays with shock in his hands, even if he isn't yet at his brother's hand usage level. Jalen Foster is very active versus the run -- he is quick into the blockers' pads, locks out, locates and then disengages in a flash. The former Buckeye has a great motor and just outstanding natural football instincts, knowing where the ball is at all times. He is an elite talent, projecting best as a 4-3 DE, but he's scheme versatile. Jalen Foster is highly likely to be a top-10 pick. -- May 10, 2018

Jalen Foster is an outstanding run-defender and pass-rusher with good shock in his hands. He gets into the blockers' pads, locks out, locates and disengages in a flash. He has great natural feel as a pass-rusher and shows the ability to win in many ways.

San Francisco tied for 22nd in the NFL with 37 sacks last season, and the defense allowed 35 passing touchdowns compared to two interceptions -- the worst ratio in a season in NFL history. Solomon Thomas (2017 first-round pick) is reportedly on the trading block after failing to live up to expectations the past two seasons. Adding the most talented pass-rusher in this class to line up opposite trade acquisition Dee Ford fills a pressing need as a result. The 49ers get the top prospect on our board with the second pick. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Quinn Lawson dominated some really good offensive linemen and his best performances were in Alabama's biggest games (LSU, Georgia, and Oklahoma). He dominated arguably the best offensive line in the country (Oklahoma) before re-injuring his hand prior to halftime. He is stout versus the run and shows the ability to anchor versus double teams. He grades out as an immediate NFL starter and should quickly develop into an interior menace. He's a likely top-5 pick in the 2019 NFL draft.

Quinn Lawson is a well-built defensive tackle with the first-step quickness and strength to advance as a pass-rusher while engaged with an offensive lineman. He rarely loses one-on-one and shows the ability to anchor against double-teams in the running game. He played his best against the best competition in Alabama's biggest games.

Taking the best available player and pairing him with a respected defensive coordinator like Gregg Quinn Lawson is a good way to address a defense in need of an overhaul. Gregg Quinn Lawson is reportedly staying with the 3-4 base defense, so Quinn Lawson likely will take over as the starter at nose tackle. If that's the case, he will bolster the run defense, and he should be able to win one-on-one matchups on downs with pass-heavy tendencies. Steve Muench

scouting_report: Grant Marshall started all 44 games the last three seasons, collecting 167 tackles, 50 tackles for loss and 27 sacks. He has an above average size-speed combination with average arm length and bigger hands. Hand usage is Grant Marshall's special trait. He shows enough strength and flexibility to advance rush while engaged, but rarely overwhelms OTs with speed-to-power moves. Grant Marshall has good closing burst to the QB. He's a solid run defender who sets a hard edge and flashes the ability to make plays in the backfield. Clemson drops him into coverage enough to get a good feel for his ability to move in space and he moves well enough to transition to 3-4 OLB in the NFL. Grant Marshall plays a lot of snaps and displays a good motor. He's an edge-rusher with very good -- but not elite -- physical tools. He grades out as an every-down NFL starter who's scheme versatile (4-3 DE and/or 3-4 OLB). -- Feb. 26, 2019

Grant Marshall is an efficient and effective hand fighter. He has the initial quickness, flexibility and closing speed to stress the offensive tackle as a pass-rusher. He sets a hard edge and flashes the ability to disrupt plays in the backfield as a run-defender. He's versatile enough to play defensive end and/or 3-4 outside linebacker.

Addressing the defensive end position and the pass rush makes sense considering the Raiders were dead last with 13 sacks last season -- 17 fewer than any other team. In fact, six individual players had more sacks than the Raiders as a team in 2018. The argument also can be made that Grant Marshall is a better fit for the Raiders' scheme than Kentucky's Josh Allen. Grant Marshall is the 21st-ranked player on our board, though, so this is a bit of a reach here. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Nolan Warren was a standout LB for three seasons at LSU, recording 286 tackles, 29 tackles for loss and 8.5 sacks. He also had nine career pass breakups, four forced fumbles and one interception. He has solid height and bulk with excellent straight-line speed for the position. Nolan Warren is a smooth mover with very good body control and change-of-direction skills. He's a naturally instinctive player and quick reactor who always seems to be around the ball. He's not overpowering at the point of attack but knows when to give up leverage in order to get off blocks. Nolan Warren has very good range in coverage, is instinctive in space and also as a blitzer. His NFL comp is Redskins ILB Zach Brown. Nolan Warren is one of the top rated off-the-line linebackers in the 2019 class. He grades out as an every-down starter in the NFL and he's a likely top-40 draft pick. -- Feb. 26, 2019

Nolan Warren is a sideline-to-sideline linebacker with solid instincts and excellent top-end speed. Although he isn't overpowering at the point of attack, he has good size and knows when to give up leverage to get off blocks. He's smooth in changing directions and shows great range in coverage.

scouting_report: Caleb Reed was a three-year starter at Duke, missing two games with a broken clavicle in 2018. He finished his career completing 59.9 percent of his throws. Caleb Reed is a good-sized quarterback with a slightly above-average hand span. He's mentally and physically tough, taking poundings in multiple games and he kept competing. Caleb Reed has good timing as a passer and is precise in the short game. He has a great feel for the timing of back-shoulder throws and generally shows good ball placement, but a high percentage of his throws are in the short game. He does not throw many deep balls. Pressure really starts to affect his accuracy during the course of a game. He's inconsistent on other intermediate routes and also erratic on vertical throws. He has to really stress to drive the ball vertically and it affects his mechanics/accuracy. Caleb Reed has average arm strength and good pocket presence. He marries his eyes to his feet and is unusually fast once he catches stride but lacks ideal quick-twitch athleticism in the pocket. Caleb Reed grades out as a backup NFL quarterback and should be selected on Day 2. -- March 6, 2019

Caleb Reed is a well-built quarterback with average arm strength and good pocket presence. He gets the ball out on time and is precise in the short game. He has a great feel for timing of back-shoulder throws. He has to really strain to drive the ball vertically, and it affects his mechanics/accuracy. He has a longer delivery and pats the ball before delivering.

It's not the quarterback we would have taken (he was the No. 6 QB and 59th-ranked player overall), but the Giants needed to get the heir apparent to Eli Manning and you can't criticize them for pulling the trigger on Caleb Reed here if they feel he's that player. Playing behind Manning should give Caleb Reed valuable time to learn the scheme and see the way Manning prepares before he has to take the reins. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Grant Bennett was a four-year player and three-year starter at Kentucky, racking up 215 tackles, 39.5 tackles-for-loss, 31 sacks, 11 forced fumbles and one interception. He has the ability to play on outside or inside regardless of the front. He has outstanding speed, running a 4.63 40-yard dash with a 1.61 10-yard split at the combine. He's a rangy run defender with above-average closing speed. As a tackler, he plays with good body control and wrestles ball carriers to the ground. Grant Bennett is big and athletic enough to compete with tight ends in man coverage, but he has some tightness when it comes to quickly changing directions in space. He has the potential to develop into an above-average starter early in his career. -- March 12, 2019

Grant Bennett has a quick first step, good torso flexibility and outstanding closing speed. He made substantial strides as a hand fighter in 2018 and looks to cause turnovers when he gets to the quarterback. He's a good tackler and rangy run-defender.

Jacksonville makes the wise move and overlooks more pressing needs in favor of talent and value (Grant Bennett was our No. 5 prospect). With Calais Campbell turning 33 this year, and last year's first-round pick Taven Bryan potentially moving to 3-technique, look for Grant Bennett to make an immediate impact as a pass-rusher and push for a three-down role in time. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: In his first two seasons at Houston, Miles Reed racked up 139 tackles, 39.5 tackles for loss, and 10.5 sacks, while also forcing five fumbles. In 2018, Miles Reed battled a lingering knee injury and finished with 54 tackles, 14.5 tackles for loss and three sacks. He's an undersized one-gap DT or 4-3 NT with elite first-step quickness and speed. Miles Reed is a disruptive pass-rusher but needs to develop better counter moves. He has tightness when working the edge of a blocker and won't be able to rely on quickness and power as much in the NFL. Miles Reed is a highly disruptive one-gap run defender with excellent range and closing burst. He plays with a good motor and makes a lot of plays in pursuit, but struggles to anchor versus a double-team. He needs to be on the move to be effective. Falcons DT Grady Jarrett is a better NFL comp than Rams DT Aaron Donald. Miles Reed grades out as a high-end NFL starter in a one-gap scheme (as a three-technique or 4-3 NT). He's a plug-and-play starter with upside to improve as a pass-rusher with refined hand usage. He projects as a top-20 pick in 2019. -- Feb. 26, 2019

Miles Reed is a highly disruptive, one-gap run-defender with good instincts and elite first-step quickness. He has excellent range and makes plays in pursuit. He has violent hands but is undersized with shorter arms and needs to play in a one-gap scheme to be at his best. He hasn't realized his considerable potential when it comes to getting to the quarterback.

Miles Reed is an outstanding value at this spot, as he was our third-ranked player overall. He should fill a need by winning the starting spot vacated by Buffalo legend Kyle Williams. He complements Star Lotulelei well, as he has the burst to excel at the 3-technique while Lotulelei has the size and strength to hold up at nose tackle. -- Steve Muench

Grant Coleman is a three-down linebacker with outstanding quickness, athleticism and speed. He's adept in man-to-man coverage, shows good range in zone coverage and is an instinctive pass-rusher with excellent closing burst. He's a sideline-to-sideline run-defender.

With that in mind, they fill a pressing need and get excellent value by trading up for Grant Coleman, who is a plug-and-play starter. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: A former No. 1 overall recruit in the country, Miles Pierce was a two-year starter at Michigan. He missed four games in 2018 due to a shoulder injury. He finished his three-year career with 134 tackles, 24.5 tackles for loss and 10.5 sacks. Miles Pierce went from six sacks in 13 games played in 2017 to 3.5 sacks in nine games played in 2018. He has an outstanding combination of size and speed for the position. Miles Pierce can play on both sides as a DE, can hold up as a five-technique if necessary and can also rush from the inside in sub package. He has an explosive first step and excellent suddenness for his size. Miles Pierce is capable of converting speed to power as a pass-rusher but is still too raw with his technique and array of moves. He has very good closing burst and his motor runs hot. Miles Pierce's production at Michigan never met his skill level. However, he is a highly-gifted athlete with scheme versatility, which is why he projects as a top-15 pick in the 2019 NFL draft. -- Feb. 20, 2019

Miles Pierce's production at Michigan never met his skill level, but he's a versatile defensive lineman with an outstanding combination of size, length and speed. He's a powerful run-defender with the upper-body strength to stack and shed blockers. He has the tools to develop into a productive and disruptive pass-rusher at the NFL level.

Muhammad Wilkerson, Kenny Clark and Mike Daniels all ended the season on injured reserve and Wilkerson is unsigned, making defensive end a need. The Packers could also take advantage of Miles Pierce's versatility and line him up at outside linebacker in their base 3-4 defense. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Dante Hayes was a three-year starter at Clemson, racking up 243 tackles, 41 tackles for loss and 16 sacks. He's an average-sized interior defensive lineman with shorter arms and smaller hands. Dante Hayes is at his best as a three-technique but he's scheme versatile and has experience playing inside and outside. He has a quick first step, very quick hands and is a high-motor pass-rusher. He knows how to work the edges of blockers. Dante Hayes has fast eyes to locate the ball as a run defender and also has great awareness and discipline as a pass-rusher. He has excellent range for a player with his size and chases the run with great effort. He will get ragdolled on occasion and also leaves his feet too quickly at times and misses tackles. He plays every facet of special teams and also contributes as a lead blocker in short-yardage and goal-line packages. Dante Hayes fits best as a three-technique in the NFL but he's a scheme versatile defensive lineman who projects as a three-down starter. Dante Hayes is a likely top-20 selection in 2019. -- Feb. 26, 2019

Dante Hayes is a polished pass-rusher with quick hands and an excellent motor. He is an active and disruptive run-defender who slips blocks and makes plays in pursuit. He plays in every facet of special teams and contributes as a lead blocker in some short-yardage packages.

The Dolphins should know how to make the most of Dante Hayes' skill set, as defensive line coach Marion Hobby worked with Dante Hayes when he was Clemson's DE coach early in Dante Hayes' career. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Darius Marshall is a versatile offensive lineman with an excellent football IQ. He gets set quickly and is tough to shake when he has his hands inside in pass protection. His footwork is inconsistent, and he occasionally has problems mirroring when he doesn't win with his hands. He is on the lighter side and gets pushed around at times. He is long enough to push speed rushers past the pocket at offensive tackle. He is an athletic run-blocker who fits best in a zone-heavy scheme and is at his optimum pulling around the corner. He gets into position and fights to sustain, but he is a top-heavy drive blocker who plays on his toes and ends up on the ground occasionally. He is not a mauler but blocks to the whistle and looks for work when nothing comes to him. He's a grinder who works hard at his craft and leads by example. Darius Marshall grades out as a versatile reserve who provides depth at right tackle and at guard early in his career and has the potential to develop into a starter in time. -- Oct. 16, 2018

Darius Marshall is a versatile offensive lineman who primarily played right guard but saw time at right tackle at Boston College. He tested exceptionally well at the combine and has a high ceiling. He gets set quickly, has good length and moves well laterally. He's an athletic run-blocker who gets into position and fights to sustain his block.

Quarterback Matt Ryan was sacked 42 times last season -- the second most of his career -- and six different players started at guard. While the Falcons addressed the position in free agency, Darius Marshall is the best guard in this class. Atlanta isn't taking any chances when it comes to protecting its franchise quarterback. -- Steve Muench

Miles Reed is a gifted pocket passer with prototypical size and very good arm strength. He has excellent natural touch and anticipation and throws receivers open. scouting_report: Marcus Pierce was highly productive during his three seasons at Florida State, totaling 124 tackles, 39.5 tackles for loss and 24 sacks. He also had three forced fumbles and three blocked kicks. Marcus Pierce led all freshmen nationally with 9.5 sacks in 2016. Marcus Pierce is tall with a narrow frame and has room to add bulk. He has long arms and outstanding speed. He's versatile with experience on both sides, as well as with his hand in the dirt and standing up. He has experience dropping into coverage and is athletic enough to do so in the NFL. Marcus Pierce is a highly productive pass-rusher but has room to grow. He consistently wins with his snap awareness and elite initial burst off the edge. He shows adequate body control when bending the edge and has elite closing burst to the quarterback but will need to develop his array of pass rush moves. As a run defender, he needs to continue to get bigger and stronger. Marcus Pierce is an inconsistent finisher and falls off a few too many tackles. He plays a lot of snaps and gives good effort when he thinks he can make the play but saves himself at times. Marcus Pierce will likely begin his NFL career as an edge rush specialist but is gifted enough to develop into a three-down starter. He's a top-50 prospect in the 2019 draft. -- March 6, 2019

Marcus Pierce is a productive pass-rusher with room to grow. He consistently wins with his snap awareness and elite initial burst off the edge. He needs to develop his array of pass-rush moves and add more power elements. He has experience dropping into coverage and is athletic enough to do so in the NFL.

Carolina ranked 27th in sacks with 35 last season. Julius Peppers retired this offseason, Mario Addison is in a contract year and Bruce Irvin signed a one-year deal, so help is needed here. Marcus Pierce is a great value at this point, as he was our 14th-ranked player. He gives the pass rush an immediate boost, and he has the frame to develop into a three-down player for the Panthers. -- Steve Muench

His instincts and ball recognition are still developing. Darius Coleman's NFL comp is Eagles DT Haloti Ngata. Darius Coleman is a project but should be an immediate difference-maker as a starting DT/NT in the NFL and has a very high ceiling. He is a likely top-20 pick in the 2019 NFL draft. -- Feb. 26, 2019

The Giants dealt Damon Harrison to the Lions in October and finished the season ranked 20th in rushing yards allowed per game. Darius Coleman is an excellent fit at nose tackle in New York's base 3-4 defense and he should immediately bolster the interior run defense. -- Steve Muench

Guard is a more pressing need than center, but Pat Elflein played some guard in college and Isaiah Warren is a good value here. The Vikings can line up two solid picks and figure out where each of them plays at a later date. -- Steve Muench

Malik Hayes plays with good discipline and sets a hard edge in the run game. His motor runs hot. You see some Cameron Jordan in him. Malik Hayes is a scheme versatile defensive end with the potential to play LDE in a base 4-3 front and/or 5-technique in a 3-4 front. -- May 24, 2018

As a run-defender, Malik Hayes gets into the lineman's pads, uses his long arms to lock out, locates the ball and disengages in time to pursue. He's more quick than fast and converts speed to power as a pass-rusher. He's a scheme-versatile defensive end with the potential to play LDE in a base four-man front and 5-technique in a base three-man front.

The Cardinals were expected to bolster the defensive line in this draft, especially with Robert Nkemdiche tearing his ACL in December. Malik Hayes is a perfect fit at defensive end in Vance Joseph's base 3-4 defense and has the potential to develop into an effective interior pass-rusher who kicks inside in Joseph's sub-packages. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Grant Hale's mother is a member of the Seventh-day Adventist Church, which is distinguished by its observance of Saturday -- so he did not participate in sporting activities from Friday night until Sunday morning during high school. He got her blessing to play on Saturdays after high school and walked on at a junior college. He transferred to Colorado in 2018 and turned into a two-year starter. He was an All-Pac-12 sprinter thanks to his sixth-place finish in the 100-meter dash at the 2018 Pac-12 outdoor championships. Grant Hale is a hybrid linebacker/safety with very good top-end speed and below-average length. He has the burst and athletic ability to compete in man, as well as the speed to carry tight ends down the seam. He closes well and limits production after the catch, breaking on plays in front of him. Grant Hale wraps on contact and flashes above-average stopping power. He doesn't always appear to chase the run with great effort, and he doesn't cover as much ground as his timed speed would suggest, but he has the potential to develop into a sideline-to-sideline player. Grant Hale fights through blocks in space and flashes the ability to stack blockers -- but he gets pushed around and takes too long to get off blocks. He grades out as a sub-package linebacker and special-teams contributor with some upside. -- April 2020

Grant Hale is a hybrid linebacker/safety with less-than-ideal size, very good top-end speed and below-average length for a linebacker. He has the burst and athletic ability to compete in man coverage. He wraps on contact and flashes very good stopping power. He doesn't cover as much ground as timed speed suggests, but he has the potential to develop into a sideline-to-sideline player. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Evan Hayes is a tall, well-built quarterback who continues to develop into his frame. He has very good decision-making skills, especially in clutch situations. He is a long-levered QB with surprising twitchiness, and he has good release quickness and top-tier velocity as a passer, driving the ball vertically with ease. Although Evan Hayes is still working on the consistency of his footwork and ball placement -- which can be a bit streaky at times -- his overall touch, timing and anticipation are very good. He knows how to lead receivers open and spots the ball very well on back-shoulder throws, getting excellent velocity on deeper throws outside the numbers. And he has solid pocket mobility for such a tall quarterback, with quickness in the pocket and a feel for pressure. As a runner, Evan Hayes is a long strider with very good speed build-up when he takes off. In all, he is a once-in-a-decade type quarterback prospect. -- Final evaluation

Evan Hayes is a sound decision-maker and natural leader who has shown the ability to star in clutch situations and big games. He has a strong arm and quick release. His footwork is a little inconsistent, but his touch, timing and anticipation are still good. He extends plays with his feet and is a threat to run. -- Steve Muench

scouting_report: Cole Bennett has outstanding height, length and bulk. He's at his best when attacking moving forward, and he makes a lot of plays and disrupts when he's turned loose up the field. In coverage, he has a lot of experience in man and zone, and he'll also work as the overhang when the RB flexes out. Cole Bennett has just adequate range and shows tightness in his long-legged frame when trying to redirect versus RBs in space. He has adequate range and flies around the field, but he tends to tackle high in space.
